bull_bear.body:
- Geopolitical disruption to supply chains and energy prices — Management explicitly flags geo-political disruptions affecting the supply chain and the effects of the West Asia war crisis on global crude prices as near-term risks; the Company's input, logistics and energy costs sit directly downstream of crude and freight economics.
- Global trade disruption and tariff uncertainty — Flagged as weighing on export demand and driving commodity inflation. With international operations across the GCC, SAARC, ASEAN and Africa contributing a rising share of volumes, tariff-driven fragmentation and localisation pressure on OEMs raise cross-border component costs and complicate the export growth strategy.
- Rising regulatory compliance cost from alternate fuel and emission mandates — Explicitly flagged as a threat. Emission and alternate-fuel transitions force continuous re-engineering and platform investment, and regulatory transition costs already weighed on H1 FY26 industry volumes.
- Tightening retail financing conditions — Flagged as potentially deferring fleet acquisition decisions. Commercial vehicle purchases are overwhelmingly financed, so buyer borrowing costs and NBFC funding conditions transmit directly into retail demand.
- Substitution risk in LCV from electric three-wheelers — Management describes competitive pressure from electric three-wheelers in select urban applications as a structural substitution risk in the near term, striking at the last-mile and urban logistics demand pool that has been the LCV segment's growth engine.
- Macroeconomic and currency volatility in key export markets — Volatility in the GCC and Africa is named as a key downside sensitivity; in FY26 political instability in Bangladesh and foreign exchange constraints in Nigeria already moderated demand and total industry volumes in those markets.
- Delayed government capital expenditure and cyclicality of infrastructure-led demand — The risk of delayed government capex is named a key downside sensitivity. FY26 M&HCV recovery was anchored in the resumption of government infrastructure expenditure and replacement of an ageing on-road fleet, so demand is tightly coupled to public spending cycles.
- Raw material price volatility and cost pass-through — Raw material trends were mixed - stable steel partly offset by volatile, upward-trending aluminium and significantly strengthened copper - requiring disciplined cost management and calibrated pricing actions; commodity inflation is also cited as an effect of trade disruption.
- Information security and cyber risk — IT and cyber risks are an integral part of the Enterprise Risk Management framework and receive focused oversight, being periodically reviewed by management and placed before the Risk Management Committee of the Board given their increasing relevance to operational resilience, data protection and stakeholder trust.

outlook.body:
- Premiumisation as an engineering commitment rather than a pricing exercise - re-engineering nameplates such as the HIPPO tractor and TAURUS tipper (320 and 360 HP) and upgrading MAV powertrains to deliver demonstrably superior total cost of ownership.
- Cost leadership through value engineering, localisation, procurement discipline and supply-base optimisation, so premium products can be priced competitively while funding R&D and protecting margins through input-cost cycles.
- Quality benchmarked to global standards across engineering specifications, supplier qualification, service standards and workshop benchmarking - described as the foundation of the premiumisation strategy.
- Building a diversified international business as the route to becoming one of the world's top 10 commercial vehicle manufacturers - deepening GCC and Africa presence, entering new countries, and localising via a wholly owned Saudi Arabian assembly subsidiary aligned with Saudi Vision 2030.
- ASEAN entry through the MOU with PT Pindad of Indonesia for joint development of electric buses and defence vehicles, broadening the geography beyond the Middle East, SAARC and Africa.
- Export-specific product design, exemplified by the Phoenix LCV built for durability, service accessibility and superior operating economics in export conditions.
- Electrification through subsidiaries - Switch Mobility India (electric buses and 2-4 tonne electric LCVs) and OHM Mobility (Electric Mobility as a Service), with real-world fleet operating economics feeding back into product development.
- Indigenous battery manufacturing via a greenfield battery pack facility at Pillaipakkam near Chennai, to reduce dependence on imported components and control a critical part of the EV cost structure.
- Three centres of eV excellence within R&D - motor/propulsion, batteries, and software for electric and autonomous vehicles (electronics and safety technologies).
- Multi-fuel technology leadership beyond battery electric - LNG, hydrogen and CNG options, with the goal of bringing alternative-fuel total cost of ownership to a level where the customer choice is straightforward.
- Selective strategic alliances in propulsion systems, powertrain electronics and safety technologies, combining Ashok Leyland's vehicle integration capability with global specialists' technology depth.
- Embedding AI across products and operations - the Uptime Solution Centre's live diagnostics and predictive maintenance, connected-vehicle data feeding product development, and AI in manufacturing quality control, supply chain optimisation and aftersales response.
- Scaling and upskilling the aftersales network - service and sales touchpoints taken to 2,104 with more than 45% of the year's additions in North and East India, plus over 2,300 Ashok Leyland Trained Technicians appointed under the ALTT programme.
- Positioning as a credible defence partner to the Indian Armed Forces across tactical and logistics vehicle categories under the Make in India and Aatmanirbhar Bharat frameworks.
- Group financial services (Hinduja Leyland Finance and Hinduja Housing Finance) retained as a meaningful contributor to consolidated performance and a demand enabler.
- Sustainability embedded in the operating model - renewable energy adoption, Zero Waste to Landfill, zero liquid discharge, and science-based decarbonisation targets.
- CSR through the Road to School and Road to Livelihood programmes, with reach being expanded towards a stated goal of one million student beneficiaries.
- Capital allocation is governed by a Board-approved Dividend Distribution Policy, hosted on the Company's website alongside its Material Subsidiary Policy, Related Party Transactions Policy, Remuneration Policy and ESOP disclosures, with the Corporate Governance framework certified by a Practising Company Secretary and MD & CEO / CFO certification furnished under the SEBI Listing Regulations. Reinvestment during the year was directed at strengthening group platforms rather than diversification: further equity subscribed in the wholly-owned Vishwa Buses and Coaches Limited, an increased stake in Optare Plc., U.K. taking holding to 93.28%, and a further investment in Gro Digital Platforms Limited. In parallel the Company is simplifying and rationalising the group - consolidating the financial services arm through the proposed merger by absorption of Hinduja Leyland Finance Limited into NDL Ventures Limited, discontinuing Switch UK's manufacturing and assembly activities at its Sherburn facility while retaining aftermarket and service support, voluntarily liquidating Ashok Leyland West Africa S.A., and seeding a new wholly owned Saudi Arabian assembly entity to localise in the Gulf.
- Enterprise Risk Management framework aligned with COSO ERM principles and ISO 31000:2018, with Risk-led Cross Functional Teams, a senior-leadership Risk Steering Committee and periodic reporting to the Board's Risk Management Committee.
- Internal Control Framework adhering to the COSO Internal Control 2013 Framework and the ICAI Guidance Note on Audit of Internal Financial Controls over Financial Reporting, operated through a Three Lines of Defense model with quarterly reporting to the Audit Committee.
- ISO27001:2022 certification for information security, supported by an independent information security function, role-based access control, periodic Segregation of Duties / Sensitive Access / End-User Access Rights reviews, and a Security Operations Center.
- Whistle-blower Policy and Vigil Mechanism providing a secure, confidential and independent channel for employees, vendors and other stakeholders to report fraud or unethical behaviour, with an Ethics Committee reviewing all ethics complaints and protection from retaliation.
- BRSR reporting for FY2025-26 on a standalone basis with Reasonable Assurance on Core Attributes from DNV Business Assurance India Private Limited.
- Commitment to extend BRSR data coverage: safety incident, water consumption, waste generation and air emissions data from Sales Offices is not reported this year, and the Company intends to implement procedures and systems to track, measure and report these parameters in future reporting periods.
- The Lucknow plant, which commenced operations only in January 2026, will have its social and environmental data reported from FY27 onwards.
- Board gender diversity of 9.09% female representation, and 8.71% female representation among permanent employees; permanent employee turnover of 7.13% in FY2025-26.
- POSH Policy and grievance redressal mechanisms in place for employees and workers, with grievance channels also extended to investors, shareholders, customers and value chain partners (the last under the Whistle-blower Policy).
- Product Safety, Quality and Innovation identified as a material responsible business conduct issue and treated as an opportunity - the Company's dedication to innovation, product safety and quality standards enhances brand value, solidifies customer trust and reduces product recalls.
- Customer Relationships and Satisfaction identified as a material responsible business conduct risk, with 6,755 customer complaints filed during FY2025-26 through the Reach Us channels and official social media accounts.

outlook.body: FY26 capacity and expansion activity was network- and internationally-weighted rather than a large domestic greenfield programme. International Operations growth was supported by selective capacity investments and deeper market engagement, with enhanced manufacturing capabilities at the Ras Al Khaimah (RAK) facility in the UAE enabling it to achieve its highest-ever production levels and reinforcing supply reliability and cost competitiveness for GCC markets. In South Africa, a strategic partnership with the Hallmark Group added 30 new touchpoints and significantly enhanced dealer coverage, while the Company initiated EV portfolio trials in select international markets and entered a strategic partnership with PT Pindad (Indonesia) for electric bus assembly and deployment under the TransJakarta programme - described as the first major step towards its ASEAN growth strategy. Domestically, the service footprint was expanded by 108 new outlets and 883 service bays, with about 40% of new outlets established in the North and East regions to improve coverage in high-potential and underserved markets, and the LCV business added 107 new touchpoints to take its dealer network to 945 touchpoints nationwide. Product-side expansion came through new platforms rather than new plants - 320 hp EGR-based tippers, AVTR 4828 multi-axle vehicles, Hippo 5532 tractors and Taurus 320 hp tippers in M&HCV, Garud 13.5M H64V, Garud 15M, Sunshine Li, Oyster CNG (School), Oyster ZMax and Oyster Max in buses, and the BADA DOST XL series which lifted addressable LCV market coverage to about 56%. On funding, the Company reported no fresh Non-Convertible Debentures issued or redeemed and no fresh External Commercial Borrowings raised during the year, availing one fresh rupee term loan while repaying scheduled instalments; management states its turnaround to a net cash position provides ample financial flexibility to fund future growth, R&D, and investments in alternative fuel and electric mobility initiatives. outlook.body:
- FY26 CV demand was two-halved: an H1 weighed down by inventory correction, regulatory transition costs and subdued freight sentiment, followed by a historic H2 recovery on post-GST 2.0 affordability, renewed infrastructure execution, strong freight demand and a robust festive season.
- The GST rate reduction from 28% to 18% in late 2025 materially lowered commercial vehicle acquisition costs, with both a direct retail CV sales impact and an indirect boost via higher logistics demand.
- Government capital expenditure and MoRTH highway construction translated directly into tipper demand at road construction, mining and real-estate sites; manufacturing GVA growth expanded industrial freight and haulage truck demand.
- Raw-material mix was uneven - steel stable with a mild softening bias while aluminium and copper strengthened, requiring disciplined cost management and calibrated pricing actions across the value chain.
- Borrowing costs for commercial-vehicle buyers softened gradually month-over-month on surplus system liquidity, improved transmission and lower NBFC funding costs.
- Bus demand normalised against a high base after SRTU fleet replacement and institutional purchases were largely executed in the prior cycle, and the electric bus transition lengthened decision cycles because of higher upfront cost, charging infrastructure and subsidy alignment.
- LCV demand was supported by e-commerce expansion, last-mile distribution, urban mobility needs and improving rural sentiment, with GST 2.0 further reducing acquisition-cost friction.
- New product launches in high-horsepower tippers, tractor-trailers and multi-axle categories are expected to help defend and strengthen market position, drive adoption in critical applications and contribute positively to segment sales growth.
- Export markets were differentiated - GCC and Africa delivered double-digit volume growth, while political instability in Bangladesh and foreign exchange constraints in Nigeria moderated demand, and Sri Lanka recovered as import restrictions eased.
- Global growth is projected to recover modestly to 3.2% in CY2027 with inflation resuming its decline, offering gradual relief on input and energy costs and supporting a measured recovery in CV demand.
- India and ASEAN are identified as the most promising growth theatres, underpinned by infrastructure investment and logistics expansion.
- Structural headwinds to be factored into international strategy: geopolitical fragmentation, aggressive Chinese OEM pricing in ASEAN and African markets, US trade policy and tariff-driven localisation pressure on OEMs.
- Margin levers cited: premiumisation and product mix, value engineering and localisation, procurement discipline and supply-base optimisation.
- AI-driven predictive maintenance and advanced safety systems are delivering double-digit gains in vehicle uptime and a 40% reduction in heavy-duty collisions across the global trucking industry, lowering fleet total cost of ownership - the metric that drives customer purchasing decisions.
- Adjacent businesses - Power Solutions, Defence, aftermarket and financial services - are positioned as contributors of both earnings and cyclical resilience.
- The defence order book and pipeline remain healthy across the Company's broader product range, with the Defence business having grown 20% year on year in FY26.
- Q4 FY26 industry demand was supported by strong export order book fulfilment for Africa and GCC markets.

deepdive.thesis: FY26 was an all-time record year (highest-ever CV volume, revenue, profit, net cash); demand was supercharged by GST 2.0 rate rationalization (~10% effective price cut) triggering an aged-fleet replacement cycle. Entering FY27 with "cautious optimism" — strong baseline/pent-up demand vs. near-term headwinds from diesel price/availability and a steel-led commodity surge. Premiumization (HIPPO/TAURUS), defence, exports, aftermarket and a now-profitable Switch EV business are the optionality layers on top of a cyclical core.

open.item: The Company is committed to carbon neutral operations by 2030, in line with the Science Based Targets initiative, and states it is on track.
The Company is committed to Net Zero emissions by 2048, in line with the Science Based Targets initiative.

The Company entered a strategic partnership with PT Pindad (Indonesia) for EV bus assembly and deployment under the TransJakarta programme, taking the first major steps towards its ASEAN growth strategy.
The Company has set a medium-term target of 25,000 export units.
Building a strong, diversified international business is central to the vision of becoming one of the world's top 10 commercial vehicle manufacturers.

The Company broke ground during Q4 FY26 on a greenfield battery pack manufacturing facility at Pillaipakkam near Chennai to build indigenous battery capability and reduce dependence on imported components.

The Company extended its Gulf presence through a new wholly owned subsidiary in Saudi Arabia - a local assembly operation for buses, trucks and commercial mobility solutions aligned with Saudi Vision 2030.
The MOU with PT Pindad of Indonesia for joint development of electric buses and defence vehicles is the Company's decisive step into ASEAN markets.
The Company will selectively pursue strategic alliances in propulsion systems, powertrain electronics and safety technologies to accelerate its product roadmap.
The Company is committed to expanding CSR reach toward its stated target of one million student beneficiaries under the Road to School and Road to Livelihood programmes.

The Company intends to extend further the premiumisation strategy that has been central to its financial performance over the past three years, defined as an engineering commitment to superior total cost of ownership rather than a pricing exercise.
Quality and cost discipline remain core operating priorities and the Company will continue to invest in both.
The stated goal is to bring the total cost of ownership of alternative-fuel vehicles to a level where the choice for the customer is straightforward.
Management states the turnaround to a net cash position gives ample financial flexibility to fund future growth, R&D, and investments in alternative fuel and electric mobility initiatives.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Ashok Leyland Limited manufactures and sells a wide range of commercial vehicles - medium and heavy trucks and buses, and light commercial vehicles - and also makes engines for industrial, powergen and marine applications, together with forgings and castings through its own Foundry Division. demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- FY26 CV demand was two-halved: an H1 weighed down by inventory correction, regulatory transition costs and subdued freight sentiment, followed by a historic H2 recovery on post-GST 2.0 affordability, renewed infrastructure execution, strong freight demand and a robust festive season.
- The GST rate reduction from 28% to 18% in late 2025 materially lowered commercial vehicle acquisition costs, with both a direct retail CV sales impact and an indirect boost via higher logistics demand.
- Government capital expenditure and MoRTH highway construction translated directly into tipper demand at road construction, mining and real-estate sites; manufacturing GVA growth expanded industrial freight and haulage truck demand.
- Raw-material mix was uneven - steel stable with a mild softening bias while aluminium and copper strengthened, requiring disciplined cost management and calibrated pricing actions across the value chain.
- Borrowing costs for commercial-vehicle buyers softened gradually month-over-month on surplus system liquidity, improved transmission and lower NBFC funding costs.
- Bus demand normalised against a high base after SRTU fleet replacement and institutional purchases were largely executed in the prior cycle, and the electric bus transition lengthened decision cycles because of higher upfront cost, charging infrastructure and subsidy alignment.
- LCV demand was supported by e-commerce expansion, last-mile distribution, urban mobility needs and improving rural sentiment, with GST 2.0 further reducing acquisition-cost friction.
- New product launches in high-horsepower tippers, tractor-trailers and multi-axle categories are expected to help defend and strengthen market position, drive adoption in critical applications and contribute positively to segment sales growth.
- Export markets were differentiated - GCC and Africa delivered double-digit volume growth, while political instability in Bangladesh and foreign exchange constraints in Nigeria moderated demand, and Sri Lanka recovered as import restrictions eased.
- Global growth is projected to recover modestly to 3.2% in CY2027 with inflation resuming its decline, offering gradual relief on input and energy costs and supporting a measured recovery in CV demand.
- India and ASEAN are identified as the most promising growth theatres, underpinned by infrastructure investment and logistics expansion.
- Structural headwinds to be factored into international strategy: geopolitical fragmentation, aggressive Chinese OEM pricing in ASEAN and African markets, US trade policy and tariff-driven localisation pressure on OEMs.
- Margin levers cited: premiumisation and product mix, value engineering and localisation, procurement discipline and supply-base optimisation.
- AI-driven predictive maintenance and advanced safety systems are delivering double-digit gains in vehicle uptime and a 40% reduction in heavy-duty collisions across the global trucking industry, lowering fleet total cost of ownership - the metric that drives customer purchasing decisions.
- Adjacent businesses - Power Solutions, Defence, aftermarket and financial services - are positioned as contributors of both earnings and cyclical resilience.
- The defence order book and pipeline remain healthy across the Company's broader product range, with the Defence business having grown 20% year on year in FY26.
- Q4 FY26 industry demand was supported by strong export order book fulfilment for Africa and GCC markets.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: FY26 capacity and expansion activity was network- and internationally-weighted rather than a large domestic greenfield programme. International Operations growth was supported by selective capacity investments and deeper market engagement, with enhanced manufacturing capabilities at the Ras Al Khaimah (RAK) facility in the UAE enabling it to achieve its highest-ever production levels and reinforcing supply reliability and cost competitiveness for GCC markets. In South Africa, a strategic partnership with the Hallmark Group added 30 new touchpoints and significantly enhanced dealer coverage, while the Company initiated EV portfolio trials in select international markets and entered a strategic partnership with PT Pindad (Indonesia) for electric bus assembly and deployment under the TransJakarta programme - described as the first major step towards its ASEAN growth strategy. Domestically, the service footprint was expanded by 108 new outlets and 883 service bays, with about 40% of new outlets established in the North and East regions to improve coverage in high-potential and underserved markets, and the LCV business added 107 new touchpoints to take its dealer network to 945 touchpoints nationwide. Product-side expansion came through new platforms rather than new plants - 320 hp EGR-based tippers, AVTR 4828 multi-axle vehicles, Hippo 5532 tractors and Taurus 320 hp tippers in M&HCV, Garud 13.5M H64V, Garud 15M, Sunshine Li, Oyster CNG (School), Oyster ZMax and Oyster Max in buses, and the BADA DOST XL series which lifted addressable LCV market coverage to about 56%. On funding, the Company reported no fresh Non-Convertible Debentures issued or redeemed and no fresh External Commercial Borrowings raised during the year, availing one fresh rupee term loan while repaying scheduled instalments; management states its turnaround to a net cash position provides ample financial flexibility to fund future growth, R&D, and investments in alternative fuel and electric mobility initiatives. qoq_log.body: - **Q4 FY26 (this call):** Record FY26 across volume/rev/PAT/net cash. Rev INR14,161 cr (+19%), EBITDA margin 14.6% (Q4) / 13.0% (FY26, +30bps). Total CV 220,437 units (all-time high). MHCV share 30.8%, LCV share 12.7% (+80bps). Net cash INR5,899 cr. Switch first-ever PAT (>INR100cr). Defence pipeline >INR1,500cr. FY27 stance: cautiously optimistic, no hard guide; steel + diesel are the watch items. Capex guide FY27 INR750–1,000 cr. New HIPPO/TAURUS impact from Q2 FY27.

thesis (one-liner): FY26 was an all-time record year (highest-ever CV volume, revenue, profit, net cash); demand was supercharged by GST 2.0 rate rationalization (~10% effective price cut) triggering an aged-fleet replacement cycle. Entering FY27 with "cautious optimism" — strong baseline/pent-up demand vs. near-term headwinds from diesel price/availability and a steel-led commodity surge. Premiumization (HIPPO/TAURUS), defence, exports, aftermarket and a now-profitable Switch EV business are the optionality layers on top of a cyclical core.

| Metric | Q4 FY26 | YoY | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | INR 14,161 cr | +19% | All-time high Q4 |
| EBITDA | INR 2,066 cr | +15.3% | All-time high Q4 |

**Volumes / market share (FY26):**
- Total CV volume **220,437 units** — all-time high (prior peak 197,366 in FY19); includes defence.
- Domestic MHCV market share **30.8%** (FY26). MHCV trucks 105,905 units (30.2% share); MHCV bus 20,840 units (34.1% share — leadership).
- Q4 domestic MHCV industry +21.5% YoY; FY26 industry +12% YoY; ALL grew in line with industry.
- LCV: Q4 21,801 units (+23% YoY, beat industry); Q4 VAHAN share 12.8% (+90 bps YoY). FY26 LCV 74,322 units (+12% YoY), share 12.7% (+80 bps) — highest-ever annual LCV.
- Exports: FY26 18,082 units (+18.5%, historic high; prior 15,255). Q4 5,322 units (marginally lower YoY — March international logistics issues).

**One-offs:** (i) Q3 FY26 one-time charge of INR308 cr for new labour code (called out; FY26 PAT figures quoted *excluding* exceptionals). (ii) Q4 had performance-related bonus provision for executives booked only after threshold reached — dampened the usual Q4 operating leverage. (iii) Q4 other/sundry income rose to INR86 cr (vs INR56 cr) on returns from surplus-fund investment.
guidance (critical):
- **M&HCV industry growth FY27:** NO hard number given — mgmt refused to "hazard a guess." Qualitative: baseline demand "very resilient"; **Q1 FY27 industry expected to be better than Q1 FY26**. Even if Q1/Q2 sees a setback, it converts to **pent-up demand** recovering in H2 (Q3/Q4). Mgmt does NOT envisage full-year industry de-growth as base case (aging fleet at all-time high + GST TCO improvement). Analysts were modeling mid-to-high single digit FY27 growth.
- **Margins:** No explicit FY27 margin guide. Q1 FY27 flagged challenging — **significant commodity cost increase, predominantly steel**; price hikes of 1–1.5% (effective Apr 1) may or may not sustain full quarter. Q4 recovered more than cost increases; Q1 gap "somewhat manageable" but wait-and-watch. Cross-functional cost teams formed (VE, e-sourcing, opex line-by-line) — benefits in subsequent quarters. Hoping for multiple price hikes across the year.
- **Market share:** New higher-HP tractor/tipper launches (HIPPO, TAURUS) shipped only a few hundred units by Mar 31; meaningful share/penetration impact expected **from Q2 FY27** (tipper + tractor-trailer segments).
- **EV ramp:** Battery pack plant (Pillaipakkam) — construction in 8–10 weeks, SOP target Q2 of next year. Switch already PAT-positive (>INR100 cr).
- **Defence:** Confident of strong growth "not just this year but next 2–3 years"; ~20% growth trend to continue.
order book / demand:
- **Defence order book >INR1,500 cr** in hand (strongest-ever pipeline), supply schedules 1–3 yrs; more orders expected during FY27.
- **Switch India order book 1,600 EV units** (from STUs + private).
- CV demand: April very positive; May no significant slowdown. Driver = GST 2.0 (~10% price cut) + aged-fleet replacement. Retail led first (LCV/ICV), fleet-owner demand surged from Dec onward. Heavy-duty retail ~55–60%, rest fleet. Fleet owners have laid out 12–18 month fleet add/replace plans and are sticking to them despite diesel noise.
- Geographic strength FY27: mining + infra (Maharashtra, Orissa, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal).
segment detail:
- **M&HCV:** ICV grew faster than HD trucks post-GST → mix pressure (HD is more margin-accretive). HD momentum building since Feb. FY27 view: tipper + multi-axle + trip-trailer (mining) fastest; tractor-trailer / non-steel-cement long-haul to moderate.
- **LCV:** Record FY26; new 4.1-ton Bada Dost (best payload); some moderation from Q4's berserk +20–25% industry levels but still > last year.
- **Buses:** MHCV bus share 34.1% — clear leadership.
- **Defence:** FY26 revenue INR1,200 cr+ incl. subsidiary (standalone books INR800 cr; Q4 INR275 cr vs INR170 cr LY), +20% YoY. Pipeline >INR1,500 cr.
- **Exports:** FY26 INR3,200 cr (crossed INR3,000 cr); Q4 INR1,100 cr (vs INR825 cr LY). Home markets GCC/Africa/SAARC demand intact; Q1 FY27 exports may dip on logistics + RAK factory production cut (recovering to 100%). Phoenix LCV launched for exports; network +4 new countries.
- **Switch Mobility:** Net profit FY26 (>INR100 cr PAT) — first-ever. EV bus leader + 2–4 ton e-LCV leader. 1,530 e-buses (+238% YoY); 1,600 e-LCVs (+56% YoY).
- **Aftermarket/Spares:** FY26 spares ~INR3,800 cr; Q4 INR1,060 cr (vs INR950 cr). Domestic aftermarket Q4 +11.2%, FY26 +9.5%.
- **Power Solutions:** FY26 ~INR1,400 cr, +16.4% YoY (Q4 engines INR425 cr, flat).
growth / optionality:
- **EV:** In-house battery business (housed in AL, part of own capex, not subsidiary); phased — pack (captive + ESS) → non-captive pack → cells. CALB partnership "on track." PLI thresholds being worked; update in 4–5 months. OHM e-bus fleet >1,400.
- **Defence:** multi-year 20% growth runway.
- **Exports:** historic-high FY26; new geographies + Phoenix product.
- **Aftermarket / Power Solutions / non-CV:** demand momentum continuing into Q1, no dip expected — de-cyclical mix.
- **HLF/HHF (financing):** HLF AUM ~INR59,000 cr (+24% YoY), PAT INR491 cr (+20%); HHF AUM ~INR16,000 cr (+15%), PAT INR387 cr (+4%); consolidated net NPA ~1.4%; growing 15–20%. HLF–NBL Ventures reverse merger to consummate this/next quarter.
margins & cost:
- Q4 material cost 71.4% (+80 bps YoY); FY26 71.4% (+10 bps). Gross margin held/improved via better realizations, value engineering, e-sourcing, commercial negotiations.
- Q4 GP improved 80 bps QoQ but did NOT translate to operating leverage (executive bonus provision + commodity surge).
- Price recovery: ~1% hike effective Jan, fully recovered in Q4. Apr 1 hike 1–1.5% by category.
- FY27 risk lines: commodity (steel-led), plus opex — chassis transportation (fuel-linked), conversion costs, FX (weak rupee). Cross-functional cost-reduction program initiated.
capex:
- Q4 capex INR203 cr; FY26 INR1,050 cr (mostly new products, future/alternate powertrains, EVs).
- FY27 capex plan **INR750–1,000 cr**.
- Battery pack plant (Pillaipakkam, near Chennai) groundbreaking done; greenfield.
capital allocation:
- Net cash INR5,899 cr (+>INR1,650 cr YoY); resolutely premiumization + fiscal discipline.
- Second interim dividend INR2.50/sh.
- Subsidiary investments Q4 INR371 cr (mainly loan repayment in offshore books; repaid GBP30m of GBP80m Optare/Switch UK loan); FY26 INR387 cr. FY27 investments on need-basis — OHM (vehicle purchases for STUs), HLF & HHF (Tier-1 capital top-up for growth) likely require funds; Switch now self-sufficient.
risks (cv cyclicality + specific):
- CV cyclicality; near-term demand wobble risk from **diesel price hikes (~INR7 so far; manageable up to INR10–15) and localized diesel availability/rationing**; war/geopolitics.
- **Commodity surge (steel, aluminum, copper, rubber)** — clear margin pressure into Q1 FY27.
- High H2 FY26 base makes FY27 comps daunting.
- Export logistics disruption + RAK factory local challenges (Q1 hit).
- Mix pressure (ICV outpacing margin-rich HD trucks).
- FX (rupee weakness) inflating costs.
management tone: Confident on FY26 record + structural demand thesis (GST + replacement cycle = resilient/pent-up demand), but deliberately **non-committal / "wait-and-watch" on FY27 numbers** and candid about commodity/diesel headwinds. Repeatedly refused to quantify guidance ("shooting in the dark"). Net: cautiously optimistic, disciplined, grounded in on-ground fleet-owner conversations.
non-obvious takeaways:
- Net cash Q3→Q4 jump (INR2,600cr→INR5,899cr) is WC seasonality (Q4 RM purchases, payables hit Apr/May) — compare YoY, not QoQ.
- GST's ~10% price benefit dwarfs the 1–1.5% hikes → pricing headroom intact without hurting demand.
- Battery business sits inside AL (own capex), NOT a subsidiary — so EV battery spend won't show as "investment in subsidiaries."
- Mgmt frames any near-term dip explicitly as *deferred/pent-up*, not destroyed demand — won't cut future-positive programs to protect short-term margin.
- "Moderation" comments are vs. the berserk Q4 GST-driven base, NOT vs. last year (volumes still expected up YoY).
challenges → potential beneficiaries:
- Steel/aluminum/copper/rubber inflation → upstream metal/commodity suppliers benefit; CV OEMs pressured.
- Diesel price hikes / availability → tailwind for EV/CNG/alt-powertrain adoption (Switch, in-house battery) over time.
- Defence indigenization (>INR1,500 cr pipeline) → AL/ALDS as beneficiary of MoD/Army orders.

themes.title: Auto OEM cycle - CV replacement & PV premiumization
themes.need: GST 2.0 rate rationalization plus an aged CV fleet still frames the replacement cycle, but Q1FY27's real signal is 2W OEMs EXPANDING margin through a commodity shock. TVSMOTOR sold 1.63mn units (+28%) on INR 13,896cr revenue (+38%) while lifting EBITDA margin 30bps to 12.8% having absorbed a ~4% commodity shock with only ~1.5% of price increase (CARE upgraded it AA+ to AAA), and committed 2W capacity from 6.8mn to 8.3mn by Q4FY27. BAJAJ-AUTO set volume/revenue/EBITDA records with margin at 20.9% (+110bps) through ~4.5% commodity inflation AND ~10% of volume lost to a ransomware shutdown, with EV now 30% of domestic revenue at double-digit EBITDA and Chetak EBITDA-positive - a scaled, profitable EV second engine. Commercial mobility is electrifying fastest: TVSMOTOR's 3W EV penetration crossed 40% for the first time. ASHOKLEY's all-time-high CV volumes (220k units, MHCV share 30.8%) carry the CV leg with defence + Switch EV optionality; TMCV/TMPV/SMLMAH/ESCORTS on CV/tractors; APOLLOTYRE/JKTYRE/BALKRISIND/MRF on tyres.
themes.driver: Capacity commissioning against demand (TVSMOTOR 2W to 8.3mn by Q4FY27, BAJAJ-AUTO 7m to 9m+ units); 3W/2W EV penetration inflection; GST-2.0 price-cut demand, aged-fleet replacement and festive 2W/PV.
